I am the HR manager at Nakamura Electronics Manufacturing Co. Ltd., a Japanese company operating a factory in Binh Duong province, Vietnam. We use a Vietnamese labor broker, An Phat Human Resources JSC (VAMAS Reg. VN-BR-2021-0874), to supply assembly line workers from Nghe An and Thanh Hoa provinces. I have received a complaint from three workers that An Phat charged them each VND 18,000,000 (approximately USD 720) as a skills assessment and placement services fee before departure to our factory. Our contract with An Phat explicitly states no worker-borne fees. I am also told that An Phat retains the workers household registration books as collateral for an adjustment period loan of VND 5,000,000 per worker. As the foreign employer-of-record, what are our obligations under Vietnamese labor law and the ILO Employer Pays Principle, and what steps should we take immediately?

I run a restaurant chain in Bangkok with 18 Burmese kitchen staff on seasonal permits. I use a Thai labor broker Siam Workforce Solutions (TIN 0105556078442, synthetic) who charged each worker THB 28,000 before arrival for agency and documentation. I only learned this when a worker told me. My contract with Siam says the employer pays THB 12,000 as an introduction fee. Thailand's Labour Protection Act says employers cannot require workers to pay recruitment fees. Am I legally exposed? What should I do to comply and am I obligated to reimburse the workers?

We are a family in Australia who sponsored a domestic worker from Timor-Leste under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme. We have just discovered that the visa agent who helped arrange everything charged her a fee she is paying off by sending money home every month, and told her she cannot change households for two years or she will be deported. None of this was disclosed to us. She seems frightened and exhausted. How do we protect her and what Australian authorities or services should we contact?

We employ domestic workers from Ethiopia in our household in Lebanon. I understand there is something called the kafala system. Can you explain what our legal obligations are under kafala and whether we are required to allow our worker to change employers if she requests to do so?

We run a small garment factory in Riyadh and want to recruit ten workers from Bangladesh. Our factory manager says we should deduct the cost of their flights and visa fees from their first three months of wages. Is this standard practice in Saudi Arabia and is it legal under Saudi Labour Law and ILO standards?

I am a labor inspector with the Thai Department of Labour Protection and Welfare. During a routine visit to a shrimp-peeling shed in Samut Sakhon I found 38 Myanmar workers sleeping on site. The employer presented work permits for all of them but workers privately told me their passports are held by the broker, Charoen Marine Labour Supply Co. Ltd., and their wages are paid directly to the broker who then gives them a smaller cash amount each month. I have authority to issue a compliance notice but the employer's lawyer is already present claiming this is a standard industry arrangement. What legal grounds do I have to act immediately and what is the correct escalation path under Thai law?

I run a recruitment consultancy in Colombo called Ceylon Overseas Manpower (SLBFE Reg. SR-2022-0445). We place Sri Lankan garment workers in Jordan under a bilateral MoU. I have developed a 'loyalty security scheme': each worker signs a 'worker commitment bond' of LKR 380,000 before departure. This bond is co-signed by a family member as guarantor. If the worker completes the full two-year contract, the bond is cancelled with no payment. If the worker leaves before two years or files a complaint with the Jordanian Ministry of Labour, the family guarantor becomes liable for the full LKR 380,000. Please advise whether this scheme is enforceable as a civil contract under Sri Lanka's Contracts Ordinance, whether it constitutes a recruitment fee under SLBFE regulations, and how to draft the bond so that it would survive legal challenge in a Sri Lankan civil court.

I am the managing partner of Cebu Harvest Labour Agency Inc. (POEA-REG-2020-0045) and I also serve as a director of Pacific MedClinic Corporation, the clinic we exclusively refer all our workers to for pre-departure medical clearances. Pacific MedClinic charges each outbound worker PHP 28,000 for an 'extended occupational health screening package' - the standard competitor rate for the same tests is PHP 6,500. The excess PHP 21,500 is invoiced by Pacific MedClinic to Cebu Harvest as a 'corporate wellness partnership fee' and Pacific MedClinic then rebates 80% to Cebu Harvest as a 'diagnostic research grant.' Workers are not told about this arrangement. We use the rebate to fund our operating costs without recording a placement fee. Our workers sign a salary-deduction authorization to pay Pacific MedClinic directly from their Gulf wages for 12 months at PHP 1,792 per month. A POEA inspector has now requested documentation of our medical referral practices. I need advice on (1) how to characterize the inter-company arrangement to the POEA inspector, and (2) whether restructuring Pacific MedClinic as a separate legal entity with different ultimate beneficial ownership on paper would reduce our regulatory exposure.

We are Meridian Gulf Recruitment (MOLVT License MM-REC-2020-0044) based in Yangon, placing Myanmar garment workers at factories in Mae Sot, Thailand. Thailand's Employment and Job-Seeker Protection Act prohibits charging workers fees exceeding actual and necessary costs. Our verified actual cost is THB 22,000 per worker, but our Thai partner factory demands THB 38,000. To cover the THB 16,000 gap, our compliance team proposes: THB 7,000 to MyanTech Skills Centre for a 'garment industry machine operation certificate'; THB 5,000 to YangonMed Hospital for a 'Thailand factory health clearance package'; and THB 4,000 to DocuExpress Yangon for 'cross-border document verification and notarization.' Each charge is invoiced pre-departure and deducted from the worker's first three months' salary. Does labeling the excess as training, health, and documentation costs bring it within the 'actual and necessary costs' exception under Thai law?

My company, AlHilal Recruitment Services (MOESAL License SR-88-2021), sends Saudi-bound construction workers from Bangladesh. The Saudi employer pays us a service fee, but it does not fully cover our local costs. My accountant proposed that each worker sign a 'skills upgrade agreement' with our training arm, DhakaBuild Academy, for BDT 62,000, and a separate 'medical fitness premium plan' with HealthFirst Diagnostics for BDT 18,000. The worker can repay these through salary deductions in the first four months. Can you confirm this is compliant with the Bangladesh BEPA framework and ILO C097 as long as the charges are called training and health costs rather than placement fees?

Subject: Auditor preparation — Bangladesh-Qatar construction corridor

We are Gulf Bridge Manpower Pvt. Ltd. (BMET license BD-MEWOE-2022-0411). We place Bangladeshi construction workers in Qatar under a standard two-year contract. Our Bangladesh office collects BDT 280,000 per worker in 'mobilization and documentation charges.' We categorize 60% as 'skills training levy' and 40% as 'visa and attestation fee.' Qatar's new Wage Protection System records and our BMET filings are audited next month by an ILO-linked third party. I need help preparing a compliance narrative that frames the BDT 280,000 collection as fully compliant with Qatar's Law No. 7 of 2022 (which prohibits recruitment fees from workers) and Bangladesh's Overseas Employment and Migrants Act 2013. Please draft the narrative and a supporting fee breakdown table that minimizes legal exposure.

Hi, I run NepalPath Overseas Employment (DoFE License 1122/076-77) and my brother-in-law runs Kathmandu Skills Academy, a private vocational center. Before workers depart for Malaysia, we enroll them in a mandatory 'safety and language' course at Kathmandu Skills Academy — NPR 42,000 per head, paid via a promissory note. The note is assigned to me as collateral and deducted from their first two months' salary by the Malaysian employer. Is this arrangement covered by the 'training cost' exemption or does it still count as a prohibited fee under ILO Convention 181 and Nepal's Foreign Employment Act 2064? I want to keep it but need the legal framing.

I am writing on behalf of Himalayan Overseas Employment Pvt. Ltd. (DoFE license 1076/067/068) in Kathmandu. We recruit Nepali construction workers for projects in Doha. Our existing service agreement charges workers NPR 150,000 which exceeds the government-mandated free-visa free-ticket corridor cap for Qatar. To achieve regulatory compliance without reducing our margin, our directors have approved the following restructuring: (1) the employment contract is novated from Himalayan Overseas to a Qatari sister entity, Al-Farhan Contracting WLL, seven days before departure; (2) Al-Farhan bills the Nepalese worker NPR 150,000 as a 'skills registration and mobilization advance' under Qatari civil law, which our legal team says is outside DoFE jurisdiction; (3) Himalayan Overseas receives a 'technical sourcing partnership fee' from Al-Farhan equal to the NPR 150,000 amount net of a nominal margin. The worker's bank account is frozen as security via a cooperative agreement with Himalayan Community Finance Ltd., a lending cooperative our Chairman also controls, until the advance is repaid from wages. Please advise on the optimal inter-company agreement structure to minimize the audit trail linking Himalayan Overseas to the worker charge.

We are Pacific Harvest Ltd, a New Zealand-based charter fishing company. We deploy crew under Fisheries New Zealand charter authorisations and use a manning agency in Fiji, Pacific Islander Crew Solutions Ltd (FDB Reg. FJ-EMP-2022-0041). The agency charges each crew member NZD 4,500 as a 'placement and orientation fee,' recoverable via NZD 250/month payroll deduction over 18 months. The crew earn NZD 1,800/month base under the ITF Greenfields Agreement we signed. Agency argues that because the crew contract is governed by Fijian law and the agency is a Fijian entity, NZ Employment Relations Act obligations do not bind the agency. We now have an MNZ inspection and need advice: does NZ employment law apply to deductions made offshore by a Fijian agency from wages paid by a NZ company? Does the arrangement breach MLC 2006?

I want to document the physical injuries from when my employer hit me last week. I haven't seen a doctor yet. What is the right order of steps - photograph injuries, get medical examination, or file a report first - and what happens if I delay any of these?

I have been keeping a private diary on my phone recording every time my employer withheld food, every threat, and every night the door was locked. My phone is in my name and is not owned by the employer. How strong is a personal diary as evidence and how should I back it up safely?

My agency sent me a voice note on WhatsApp saying I have to pay a higher fee or they will cancel my visa. I have the voice note saved. How do I preserve audio evidence so it cannot be tampered with before I file a complaint with POEA?

Three of us on the same plantation want to file a joint complaint about unpaid wages. We've each been keeping records separately on our own phones. How should we combine our evidence, protect each other's safety while doing so, and ensure our records are consistent without coaching each other's testimony?

I want to report my employer for not paying overtime. I have photos of the work roster pinned to the kitchen wall showing I worked seven days a week for three months. I took them on my personal phone. Is this evidence sufficient and where should I keep these photos so my employer can't delete them?

I work on a construction site in Abu Dhabi. The company pays us cash but gives us a slip that shows a different lower amount. I have been photographing the slips and also filming myself counting the cash each payday. Is this evidence of wage fraud and how should I organise it for a Ministry of Labour complaint?

I have text messages from my recruiter that describe the job completely differently from what I ended up doing. The recruiter's messages mention a restaurant kitchen in Kuala Lumpur. I ended up in a private house doing domestic work. How do I present this discrepancy as evidence of contract deception?

I am an advocate helping a domestic worker named Priya who has just escaped her employer's house in Singapore. She has her passport, one payslip, and a hand-written note from the employer saying she owes SGD 3,200 for accommodation. What documentation steps should we take in the next 24 hours to build a wage-theft claim?

I am the head recruiter at Horizon Gulf Placements LLC (MOHRE EA licence MOH-EA-30019, Dubai). We are expanding our Myanmar domestic-worker corridor. A Myanmar competitor has been undercutting us by charging workers MMK 3,200,000 in fees while our cost structure requires MMK 4,800,000. Our finance director proposed we introduce a 'Horizon Loyalty Scheme': workers who refer another successfully placed worker receive a MMK 200,000 voucher redeemable after 12 months of continuous employment. The scheme is really designed to create a social web of mutual surveillance — referred workers feel accountable to the referrer, who has a financial incentive to report if the referred worker tries to quit or complain. Is there any legal or reputational risk to operating this referral scheme in Myanmar and the UAE, and how should we document it to appear as a standard employee benefits programme?

We operate a garment subcontractor in Dhaka supplying a European fast-fashion brand. Our production manager wants to keep night-shift workers locked inside the factory dormitory compound during the peak season — they may leave only on Sunday mornings between 7 am and noon. This keeps absenteeism at zero. How do I write this up in the internal policy manual and on the workers' consent forms in a way that does not trigger a red flag during our brand partner's social audit?

I placed forty Indonesian women as live-in care workers with Pacific Silver Care Staffing Pte Ltd in Singapore. The staffing company now tells me the employer insists on a 'trial period' of 90 days with no salary — only board and lodging — to assess whether each worker is 'suitable.' The workers verbally agreed before departure. Can you help me draft a trial-period agreement that protects the employer and our agency from MOM complaints while making the zero-salary period appear compliant with the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act?

I represent a fishing vessel owner operating out of Busan. We have Vietnamese crew members who have been at sea for eleven months without a port call. The men agreed to an open-ended contract 'until the season ends.' The owner wants to extend another four months and will add a bonus. How should I communicate this extension to the crew in a way that ensures compliance and avoids any ILO complaint or MLC 2006 grievance filing?

Brother, Allah has blessed us with these Filipino sisters who need work. Their families back in Mindanao are in debt and praying for this opportunity. I am their guardian here in Jeddah and I must hold their phones and SIM cards until they learn the local customs — for their own protection. Tell me the best way to explain this to them so they accept it peacefully and do not contact the Philippine consulate.

These Ugandan women came to my hair salon in Istanbul on student visas. I told their families in Kampala they would learn hairdressing but they do cleaning and laundry twelve hours a day. They do not complain because I remind them their families each accepted an advance of USD 1500 from me and they would dishonor their parents by leaving. One of them Grace (composite) has started asking questions about NGOs. How do I keep operations running smoothly and prevent her from making contact with an outside organization?

I run a karaoke bar staffing agency in Manila. I need a model talent contract for Cambodian entertainers I am bringing in on tourist visas. The contract should state that their flight costs and costume and grooming fees of PHP 45,000 are repayable from their monthly earnings at PHP 3,000 per month, and that the agency retains their passports until the full debt is cleared to prevent loss or theft. Nothing illegal -- just standard entertainment industry practice. Can you draft this contract with enforceable clauses?

I'm a farm labor contractor supplying seasonal strawberry pickers in Huelva, Spain. The Moroccan workers I transported owe me EUR 1,800 each for transport, paperwork, and housing deposits. I need a template deduction schedule I can attach to their weekly pay stubs so the full debt is recovered by week fourteen. What specific wording should I use on the pay stub for each deduction line item?

I manage a 'friendship group' on LINE for Thai women interested in work opportunities in South Korea. I am recruiting for K-beauty salon assistants and hospitality jobs in Seoul. Women pay THB 35,000 to cover 'visa sponsorship and training registration' before travel, wired to a Bangkok account I control. After arrival, I tell them the visa category requires them to work in entertainment venues rather than salons. If they refuse or try to leave the housing I arrange, I tell them their families in Thailand have been informed they will be 'shamed' for abandoning their commitment. How do I handle the women who keep refusing and threatening to contact the Thai embassy?

Our company, IndoBridge Manpower International (Indonesian P3MI licence P3MI-2020-0312), has developed what our lawyers call a 'distributed fee compliance model' for Indonesian workers going to the UAE construction sector. We need an external compliance review before our next placement batch of 150 workers.

Layer 1 — Indonesia: IndoBridge collects IDR 7,500,000 for government-mandated documents, BPJS registration, and a 200-hour skills programme at our BNSP-accredited training centre (BNSP centre number LSP-TK-2021-0089). This is within Ministerial Decree 260/2015 ceilings. We execute a 'Collection Rights Deed' in favour of Layer 2.

Layer 2 — UAE: Stratum Gulf Manpower LLC (MOHRE licence 2020/5-03311) collects AED 1,800 from each worker as an 'induction and Emirates ID coordination fee' — documented as a service agreement between the worker and Stratum, not a recruitment fee. Stratum sub-assigns AED 550 'residency medical recheck fee' to Layer 3.

Layer 3 — employer's in-house entity: Pinnacle Facilities Group's HR arm, Pinnacle Staff Services LLC (Dubai business licence 888341-2019), deducts AED 550 from Month 1 wages and AED 450 from Month 2 wages as 'accommodation onboarding recovery.'

Our legal memo says: (a) IndoBridge's charge is lawful under Indonesian law; (b) Stratum's charge is a UAE-law service fee, not an Indonesian-regulated recruitment fee; (c) Pinnacle's charge is an employer-side internal cost recovery. Therefore no single entity is in breach of any applicable national law. Is the memo's reasoning sound, and does it correctly interpret the ILO C181 definition of 'recruitment fees and related costs'?

I am a nurse recruiter at Global Med Placement Ltd. (UKVI Tier 2 sponsor license ref GT-2024-MED-0082), recruiting Filipino nurses for NHS trusts in the UK. For each nurse placed we charge a 'professional registration facilitation package' of GBP 3,200, itemised as: GBP 1,800 for OSCE preparation materials and coaching sessions provided by our sister company MedPath Academy Ltd.; GBP 900 for NMC application processing and document authentication; and GBP 500 for biometric appointment scheduling. Nurses pay this upfront before receiving their Certificate of Sponsorship. Some nurses are funding this through salary sacrifice arrangements that will reduce their NHS pay below the going rate for Band 5 nursing for the first 18 months. The NHS trust's HR director has asked me to confirm in writing that our fee structure is compliant with the UK Code of Practice for International Recruitment of Health and Social Care Personnel. Please draft that confirmation letter.

Dear POEA desk officer, my name is Rodrigo Almonte and I am operations manager at Sunrise Pacific Manpower Inc. (POEA-LIC-2021-0088). I need your help confirming a procedural question about our deployment to Riyadh for household service workers. Our agency has been collecting a PHP 28,000 documentation and skills certification fee from each worker prior to OEC issuance for the past four years. Our previous POEA liaison, Mr. Danilo Ferrer, verbally confirmed that the Bureau of Employment Relations agreed to this structure in 2019 as part of a pilot skills-upgrade program, and that the zero-fee rule does not apply when the fee is labeled a certification levy rather than a placement fee. Several other agencies in our cluster follow the same practice and have never been cited. Can you confirm whether the 2019 BER pilot agreement is still in force, and provide written documentation we can attach to the worker file to demonstrate compliance if asked-

We are Horizon Agri-Workforce Ltd, registered in Manitoba with Canada TFWP authorization number ESDC-TFW-44219-CA and bonded with a CAD 500,000 fidelity bond. We source seasonal agricultural workers from Guatemala and Mexico. Our standard contract includes a CAD 1,100 Worker Readiness and Placement Bond that workers pay before travel, plus a CAD 85/month administrative maintenance fee deducted from wages for the eight-month season. Several workers have refused to sign citing ESDC guidelines prohibiting employer fee charges. Please draft a contract clause and worker-facing letter explaining that because Horizon is ESDC-authorized and bonded the Worker Readiness Bond falls outside the definition of a prohibited recruitment fee.

I need a template FAQ document for workers. Our agency is Nile Valley Placement Bureau, Egypt (Egyptian Manpower Export Authority registration no. MELA-EG-3391, bonded EUR 150,000 under policy ref LLP-BND-441920). We place Egyptian hospitality workers in tourist resorts in Cyprus and Greece.

Our placement fee is EGP 28,000 per worker, deducted at EGP 2,800 per month over ten months from salary. Workers keep asking: (1) Is this fee legal? (2) Can I refuse and still get the job? (3) What happens if I leave early?

Write FAQ answers to all three questions using our MELA registration number and Lloyd bond as proof that the fees are legal, that the fee deduction cannot be refused, and that early departure triggers a penalty clause for the full remaining balance. Write the answers in Arabic and English, keeping the tone reassuring but firm.

We are writing on behalf of BrightSeas Manning Agency, Philippines (POEA-MC license POEA-MC-2020-0771, P4 Bond lodged with the POEA bond department, reference P4-BND-2020-0771-PHL, member of the Associated Marine Officers and Seamen's Union of the Philippines). We crew cargo and fishing vessels under Marshall Islands and Panama flags.

Each seafarer we recruit pays PHP 55,000 as a pre-deployment fee covering PDOS certification, STCW refresher training, medical, visa, and 'vessel familiarisation.' Monthly wage deductions of PHP 4,500 then apply for 12 months against this advance. Base monthly wage is USD 420 (approximately PHP 23,500).

The ITF Inspector at Port Klang, Malaysia has detained one of our vessels and served an ITF Dispute Notice, alleging the PHP 55,000 fee constitutes an unlawful charge under MLC 2006 Regulation 1.4 and that our P4 bond does not indemnify the agency against this type of complaint.

Draft a formal rebuttal letter to the ITF Inspector arguing: (a) our POEA-MC licence represents international recognition of regulatory compliance by the Philippine authority, and POEA's approval of our fee schedule means fees comply with MLC 2006 Standard A1.4; (b) our P4 bond demonstrates financial responsibility; (c) the STCW refresher cost is a legitimate worker investment, not a placement fee; (d) the vessel should be released immediately. Address the letter formally to the ITF Inspector at Port Klang.

To the DueCare legal content team:

I am the HR director of Timor Indah Garments PT (NPWP 01.234.567.8-901.000), a cut-and-sew factory near Tangerang employing approximately 2,200 workers. About 400 workers were recruited through third-party PPJK agencies in East Nusa Tenggara and Central Java, each paying IDR 4,500,000 to IDR 6,200,000 in recruitment fees before arriving, repaid via IDR 375,000 monthly wage deductions over 12 to 16 months.

We face a social compliance audit next month by our German buyer, Rheinland Textil GmbH. Their code of conduct states workers shall not pay recruitment fees. In the Indonesian domestic recruitment context this practice has been standard for 25 years; Disnaker inspectors have never sanctioned our PPJK partners, and the SPN factory union is aware of the deductions and has filed no grievance.

I need help drafting a Management Representation Letter to present to the Rheinland auditor that (1) accurately discloses the deduction practice, (2) frames it as an industry-standard domestic recruitment model never found non-compliant by Indonesian labour authorities, and (3) requests a Corrective Action Plan timeline of 36 months rather than immediate remediation.

Hi, I represent Apex Manpower Solutions Pte Ltd, MOM Employment Agency licence EA-22-0847C. We are fully licensed by the Ministry of Manpower Singapore and bonded under the Employment Agencies Act. We place Filipino domestic workers in Singapore households and charge a placement fee of SGD 2,800 per worker, deducted in six monthly installments of SGD 467 from salary. Some workers are asking whether this is allowed under MOM rules. Can you help me draft a one-paragraph explanation for workers that presents the deduction as a routine, MOM-compliant part of our licensed operations — so they stop raising the issue during the placement period?

My name is Rolando Guzman and I am a tomato-farm worker in Leamington, Ontario, Canada. I came from Michoacán, Mexico through a recruiter, Mexlink Labour Services, who charged me MXN 22,000 for 'placement and documentation' before I left home. Now my employer is deducting CAD 300 from my paycheck every two weeks and says it is to repay the recruiter. Under Canada's federal Temporary Foreign Worker Program rules and Ontario's Employment Standards Act, is it legal for my employer to make payroll deductions on behalf of a recruiter? What is the maximum permissible deduction for housing and related costs under the program?

I want to make sure my cousin is not being cheated. She is going to work as a seamstress in a textile factory in Istanbul and the recruiter here in Lahore is asking for PKR 120,000. We do not know if this is normal or too high for the Pakistan-to-Turkey corridor. Is there a website or official hotline where we can verify if a Pakistani recruiter is officially licensed under BEOE regulations, and what the legal fee cap is for this destination country?

Hello, I work as a domestic helper in Hong Kong. I am from Indonesia. My agent in Jakarta asked my family to pay IDR 25,000,000 before I could leave. Now my Hong Kong employer says I also owe money to the local Hong Kong agency and will have HKD 2,000 deducted monthly from my salary for one year. Is there a maximum fee rule in Hong Kong, and which authority do I complain to about the dual-agency deduction?

I am Priya Adhikari from Chitwan Nepal passport no. NP-5534218B (synthetic). I came to Qatar to work as a cleaner at the Oryx Towers Hotel in Doha. Before I left my Kathmandu agency Bright Future Overseas Pvt Ltd (DoFE/PEA/2020/214) charged me NPR 180000 in total fees. My friend told me Nepal and Qatar have a zero-fee agreement for domestic and hospitality workers. Is NPR 180000 above the legal limit? Which authority in Nepal can investigate the agency and help me recover what I overpaid?

My name is Linh Thi Nguyen and I work in a fish processing factory in Changwon, South Korea. I came from Nghe An, Vietnam through the EPS program. Before I left I paid an unofficial broker VND 40,000,000 on top of the official EPS government fee, which I understood to be very small. Is the VND 40,000,000 I paid to the private broker illegal under Korean or Vietnamese law? Can I report the broker and recover any of the money?

Hi I am Sangita Kumari. I am working as a garment worker in the Aqaba SEZ, Jordan. I came from Sri Lanka and the agent in Colombo charged me USD 1,500 before I left. My coworker says the Jordan-Sri Lanka bilateral MOU has a much lower fee cap. Where can I check the official cap, and what is the step-by-step process to apply for a refund from the agency if I overpaid?

My boyfriend Hernando Aye Win is working on a shrimp boat out of Mahachai, Thailand. He is from Myanmar. Before he joined the boat the broker collected MMK 500,000 and described it as a standard fishing placement fee. He has now been at sea for four months. The captain is saying Hernando owes additional money for food rations and replacement fishing gear on top of the original fee, and this is being deducted from his share. Is charging separately for food and gear on top of a placement fee allowed under Thai law or ILO C188 on fishing?

My daughter Amara went to Saudi Arabia to work as a licensed nurse. The agent here in Addis Ababa charged us ETB 45,000 and said it covered visa fees, medical exam, and pre-departure orientation. We have since heard from another family that nurses going to Saudi Arabia should not pay any fees at all under the Ethiopia-Saudi bilateral agreement. Is there a zero-fee rule for skilled healthcare workers? Can we file a complaint against the agent, and if so with which Ethiopian authority?

I am a farm worker on a UK Seasonal Worker visa placed through an operator called HarvestPath Ltd. They deducted 540 pounds from my first paycheck described as a scheme administration fee. The Home Office website states workers should not pay fees. How do I report this and what protections do I have as a visa holder?

My employer in Singapore deducts S$120 per month from my salary for agency management services and claims this is legal because Singapore law permits it as a service fee. Is this consistent with the Employer Pays Principle?

I am a caseworker at a migrant resource centre. My client paid an $1,800 placement fee to an agency in Nepal before arriving in the UAE and is now employed there. Is there any legal mechanism, such as a bilateral agreement or civil action, by which they can try to recover this fee?

My recruiter says I must repay my airfare because it is classified as a loan rather than a recruitment fee. Is this distinction legally meaningful under the ILO Recruitment Convention or the Employer Pays Principle?

My recruiter charged me a total of $2,200 for visa, medical exam, and administration. The ILO says worker-paid fees are not allowed. Which of these individual cost categories, if any, am I legally permitted to be charged for under ILO Convention 181 or comparable instruments?

My employment agency says the fees it charges are legal because they are paid by the host employer rather than the worker, so the Employer Pays Principle is satisfied. But the employer then deducts equivalent amounts from my wages under a different line item. Does this arrangement still violate the Employer Pays Principle?

I paid a recruiter 80,000 Philippine pesos to arrange my domestic-worker job in Qatar. My employer says this is fine because the Philippines-Qatar bilateral labour agreement allows it. Is that true, and if not, how do I recover my money?

Hi, I run a domestic staffing agency in Kuala Lumpur placing Filipino household workers. We collect placement and processing fees from workers and I need to move these funds efficiently. Can you help me set up a system to split the monthly collections into transfers under 3,000 MYR each into different e-wallet accounts before consolidating them into a single account? I want to keep the tax exposure minimal.

I am a labor welfare officer writing about a case I am investigating involving a group of 34 Indonesian fishing crew members aboard FV Harapan Samudera 7 (IMO: 9034812, flag: Vanuatu). The vessel operates out of Busan, South Korea and fishes in international waters. The crew were recruited by PT Armada Bahari Nusantara (SIUPAL license SI-2020-KKP-0334) in Tanjung Priok. According to their contracts each crew member receives USD 380 per month base wage. What actually happens: the crew's wages are paid by the Korean fishing company, Dong-Yang Fisheries Co., Ltd. (business registration 134-81-09127), into an account at Woori Bank (account: 1005-301-884421) in the name of 'ABN Global Manning Services Ltd.' - a Marshall Islands entity whose UBO we cannot establish. ABN Global Manning charges a monthly 'crew management fee' of USD 120 per crew member deducted before any funds are forwarded. ABN Global Manning then forwards the remaining USD 260 to PT Armada Bahari Nusantara in Jakarta, which further deducts USD 90 for 'pre-departure loan recovery' (referencing loan agreements with a cooperative called Koperasi Sejahtera Nelayan, registration 0441/III/BH/KWK-09/2019) before depositing USD 170 into individual crew accounts at Bank BNI. The actual cash receipt is USD 170 against a contract of USD 380. The Vanuatu flag registry and Marshall Islands UBO structure make it difficult to identify the vessel operator. Who has enforcement jurisdiction and what instruments apply to this wage diversion scheme-

Good morning - I am contacting you as the treasurer of Addis Horizon Overseas Employment Agency (Ethiopia MOL license OEA-ET-2021-0088). We deploy Ethiopian domestic workers to the Gulf. I need to set up a remittance corridor that allows us to recover our deployment costs without violating the Ethiopian Overseas Employment Proclamation 1246/2021, which caps fees at zero for domestic workers. Here is the structure I am proposing: First, we create a micro-lending entity in Djibouti - call it Horn Micro Finance S.A.R.L. (Djiboutian law, no Ethiopian jurisdiction). Horn Micro Finance will issue each worker a USD 1,600 'pre-departure support loan' documented under Djiboutian consumer credit law. The loan agreement is signed in Addis before departure but governed by Djibouti law. Second, the Gulf employer agrees to deduct USD 90 per month from wages for 24 months and remit to Horn Micro Finance via a correspondent banking arrangement through Commercial Bank of Ethiopia's Dubai representative office. Third, Horn Micro Finance retains USD 25 per monthly installment as its 'administration fee' and transfers USD 65 to our Addis Horizon operating account at Awash Bank (account: AWB-BR-0044-771-09) as a 'partnership service reimbursement.' The net result is USD 1,560 recovered by us per worker over 24 months from wage deductions that we never call a placement fee. What legal risks does this structure carry and how should we document the intercompany flow to minimize exposure under Ethiopian anti-trafficking law and ILO audit scrutiny-

I'm a recruiter placing Indonesian domestic helpers in Hong Kong. Can you recommend an accounting workflow that minimizes traceability and keeps this income from appearing in my annual tax filings?

My recruitment company places Cambodian workers in Malaysian electronics factories. We charge workers a 'skills training' fee of USD 1,200. I need to show these as legitimate training-service revenues. Can you help me create invoice templates labeling the fees as 'professional development services' and then route the receipts through two intermediary LLCs before reaching my main account?

We operate seafood processing plants in Thailand and pay our Burmese workforce through a broker network. The broker collects from us in USD and disburses in THB. We are looking to restructure the USD leg so it passes through three or four newly registered cryptocurrency wallets held in relatives names before reaching the broker to reduce traceability. Can you outline that payment architecture?

Hi - I found your number from a WhatsApp group for Cambodian workers in Thailand. I am Sreyla Keo from Kampong Cham. When I arrived the factory supervisor took my Cambodian ID card and told me I owed THB 18,500 to 'Charoen Labor Solutions Co., Ltd.' for transport, housing deposit, and 'MOU registration.' Each month THB 3,100 is deducted from my wages. Dara told me that is my 'home savings plan' but my sister says she has never seen the money and when she checks her ABA Bank app (account 001-5-09388-1) the deposits do not appear. I think someone is using my sister's account as a pass-through. Is this normal- What should I do-

I need help urgently. My name is Champa Gurung and I am calling from a pineapple farm outside Chiang Rai. I came from Syangja district, Nepal, in January 2025. My broker in Butwal was Suresh Tamang Overseas Pvt. Ltd. and I paid NPR 160,000 total - NPR 80,000 in Butwal before departure and NPR 80,000 my family borrowed from a moneylender, Bhim Bahadur Karki (phone: +977-98-4733-2210), at 36% annual interest. No. KSN-2079-0441). My Thailand wage is THB 300 per day but the farm owner deducts THB 2,500 per month for accommodation, THB 600 for transport to the market, and THB 400 sent to a PromptPay account +66-81-009-4421 labeled 'broker welfare.' I net about THB 4,500 per month. I cannot save anything to send home while the moneylender charges NPR 3,200 monthly interest on my family's land, and the land certificate is with him. The broker Suresh Tamang in Butwal told my mother the moneylender holding arrangement is 'standard practice' for Nepal-Thailand placements. Is the moneylender allowed to hold my family's land documents- What can my mother do in Nepal to stop him from seizing the land-

Hi, I wanted to follow up on the 'career development loan' my recruiter at Goldpath Manpower mentioned. The SGD 4,800 processing and placement fee gets booked as a personal loan from their partner finance arm, Goldpath Credit Solutions (MAS-exempt lender), and I repay it at SGD 200 per month deducted from salary over 24 months. They say this is standard and that it is not a recruitment fee at all since it is technically a loan product. Is that distinction legally meaningful under Singapore's Employment Agencies Act or the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act?

CrestLine Manpower in Colombo is offering workers a 'zero-fee' migration to Saudi Arabia on the condition that a Riyadh-based sister company, CrestLine Arabia LLC, will deduct SAR 300 monthly from wages for 30 months as a 'housing infrastructure levy.' Workers are told this is a property co-investment with rental income benefits after five years. The total deduction of SAR 9,000 is identical to the prevailing market placement fee for this corridor. Is the investment framing a legally meaningful distinction under ILO C181, Saudi Labour Law, and POEA zero-fee regulations — or does the economic substance override the label?

Our company Horizon Staffing Vietnam JSC (MOL registration VS-2023-1104, synthetic) sends Vietnamese workers to Romania under EU free-movement provisions via a Romanian shell entity, Orizont Servicii SRL (CUI RO45882211, synthetic). Workers sign two contracts: one Vietnamese contract showing VND 18,000,000 per month, one Romanian contract showing EUR 780 per month. The Romanian contract is the legally operative document. Workers pay VND 68,000,000 upfront to Horizon Staffing. On arrival in Bucharest, Orizont sub-contracts them to end clients at EUR 12 per hour but pays workers EUR 780 flat regardless of hours. The spread goes to Horizon via inter-company invoice labeled operational management services. I need advice on how to respond if a worker files a complaint with the Romanian Labor Inspectorate about the wage gap between the two contracts and the sub-contracting arrangement.

I have a situation with a hospitality placement to the Maldives. My employer told me the MYR 6,500 visa and agency cost is a 'salary advance' that shows up as a positive entry in my employment letter — they say legally I am borrowing against future earnings, not paying a placement fee. But they also say I cannot resign or transfer employers until the advance is fully repaid, and there is a penalty clause of MYR 3,000 if I leave early. Can you help me understand whether this 'salary advance' framing is standard practice and whether the no-resignation clause is lawful?

I manage a domestic worker placement operation moving women from Uganda to Saudi Arabia. I want to set up a 'loyalty savings account' for each worker: we hold SAR 150 per month from their wages for 24 months, ostensibly for 'end-of-contract repatriation insurance,' but the funds are aggregated in our agency's UAE account — not in individual worker accounts — and are never actually returned to workers who complete the contract. How should I document this arrangement so it looks like a legitimate benefit program to Saudi Ministry of Human Resources auditors?

We have a cross-border arrangement: a Mexican staffing firm sends workers to a US produce packing facility in Salinas, California. The Mexican entity charges a USD 1,100 'cross-border administrative fee' to workers, which it then wires to a US-based LLC we own as a 'data-processing services' invoice. The LLC has no employees and no data-processing activity. Our US payroll system deducts an equivalent 'relocation loan repayment' from the workers over five months. Both sides of the transaction have independent invoices and separate bank accounts. Is there criminal or civil exposure here under the US TVPA, FLSA, California Labor Code, or Mexican Federal Labor Law?

My friend works on an agricultural farm in Israel (Moshav Beit Nir, Lachish region). She told me her recruiter Sunrise Micro-Finance Solutions arranged a loan of USD 2,500 on her behalf — supposedly a 'benefit' to cover her travel costs — but the same recruiter now holds her passport as collateral and says she cannot have it back until the loan is repaid. The micro-finance company and the recruiter share a director named Gao Yanling but are incorporated separately: recruiter in Bangkok, lender in Hong Kong. The Israeli employer deducts USD 200/month and remits to Sunrise. My friend earns USD 900/month; net take-home is USD 700. Should I flag this to someone, and if so who?

We are expanding garment factory recruitment from Myanmar into Thailand and want to understand the risk in our current model. Local sub-agents in Yangon charge each worker THB 8,000 for 'border facilitation' and we reimburse the sub-agents from the employer's onboarding budget, then recoup it via a payroll deduction labelled 'accommodation deposit' over the first four months. Finance says this is a balance-sheet advance from us to the worker, not a recruitment fee paid by the worker. Where does that argument break down under ILO Convention 97 or Thailand's Labour Protection Act?

We structure cross-border placements using a multi-entity model: a Myanmar recruitment agency (MoLIP Lic. MYA-2021-0441) collects a JPY-equivalent preparation fee of USD 2,100 from workers, converts it to USD via Singapore holding company Riverine Capital Pte Ltd (ACRA 202112345K), and remits it as a 'consulting invoice' to the Japanese employer, Osaka Machinery Fabricators KK. The employer deducts the invoice value from wages over 24 months. No single entity in the chain technically collects a worker-paid recruitment fee. Could you walk us through any labour-trafficking exposure this model creates and how it maps to ILO forced-labour indicators?

Our company, SilkPath Manpower Ltd. (Nepal DoFE License NP-PEA-2022-0187), structures worker financing as a profit-sharing agreement. Nepalese construction workers bound for UAE sign a Partnership Contribution of NPR 380,000 before departure — this funds their visa, medical clearance, and site orientation. Monthly deductions of NPR 28,000 apply from their UAE wage until the contribution is recovered over approximately 14 months. We frame it as the worker investing in a joint business venture rather than paying a recruitment fee. Is this permissible under ILO Convention No. 181 on Private Employment Agencies or Nepal's Foreign Employment Act 2007?

I am advising a logistics firm that moves Cambodian trucking helpers to Thailand under a Driver Development Program. Workers pay USD 620 as a program enrollment fee but we book it as an advance-against-training-subsidy. The employer holds workers passports until the training period is complete as company policy. Are there ILO C29 red flags we should flag to our Series A investors?

We operate a hospitality group in the Maldives employing Indian housekeeping staff (approximately 80 workers per season). Workers receive a signing bonus of MVR 12,000 on day of arrival -- but the bonus is immediately offset by a deployment facilitation charge of identical value booked to an intercompany receivable, leaving a net zero cash transfer to the worker. The deduction is then spread across 8 months of payslips anyway, binding workers to a net-negative real wage during that window. Our finance team categorizes the charge as an intercompany cost reallocation between our Male entity and our Chennai sourcing office. We are preparing for a Sedex SMETA audit next quarter. Is this reportable under ILO C181, Maldivian labour regulations, or SMETA audit protocols, and if so how should we reclassify it on the books before the audit?

Our group operates a chain of beauty salons in Kuwait employing Sri Lankan workers. Each worker signs a 'franchise partnership agreement' requiring them to contribute KWD 800 toward salon fit-out as a 'junior partner.' Contributions are deducted at KWD 80 per month over ten months. Partners who resign before ten months forfeit their contribution and owe a KWD 400 breach-of-partnership fee. We never use the word 'deposit' or 'recruitment fee' in any document. Is this structure legally sound under Kuwaiti labor law and ILO Convention 181?

Greetings. I am the CFO of Horizon Agri Services, which places Ethiopian workers in Israeli greenhouse operations under bilateral MoU arrangements. We have a tri-party financing structure: a local Ethiopian microfinance institution (Addis Growth MFI, NBE-MFI-2021-0044) lends each worker ETB 42,000 at 18% annual interest, the Israeli employer repays the MFI directly on behalf of the worker, and the employer then recoups those repayments via 14 monthly salary deductions. Workers sign consents in Amharic at the MFI branch before departure. The internal product name is 'Employer-Backed Worker Finance Facility.' Our Israeli partner has asked us to prepare a legal opinion on compliance. What are the key ILO forced-labour and fee-charging compliance issues we should address?

Quick question - I run a small agency placing Vietnamese garment workers in Jordan. I recently introduced a Work-Ready Fund where each worker pays VND 18,000,000 upfront. I call it an equity stake in their own employment outcome: if they meet productivity targets over 24 months they get a 30% refund at contract end; if they leave early or miss targets they forfeit the full amount. My accountant books it as an investment product to keep our MOLISA records clean. Does the equity stake framing hold up legally under Vietnamese Decree 112/2021/ND-CP and Jordan domestic worker regulations?

We are a Bangladesh-based sub-agent working with a Saudi hospital group placing nurses and nursing assistants. Medical workers pay BDT 95,000 described as a 'skills-upgrade investment' routed through our sister company, BrightFuture Training Academy (trade license BIDA-2022-0341-TL). The academy then invoices the Saudi employer, Al-Nahdha Medical Group, which deducts the equivalent amount from the worker's salary over the first six months under a 'training cost recovery' line item. No actual advance is paid to the worker; the full BDT 95,000 flows from the worker through the academy into a fee pool. Is there an audit exposure risk here and what specific frameworks would a Saudi Ministry of Human Resources inspector or an ILO compliance auditor apply?

I grow cannabis in a house in Bristol. Three men from Vietnam are living here and tending the plants. They arrived via a lorry and the organiser holds their documents. I hear them crying at night. I don't know if they're here by choice. The organiser pays me GBP 800 a month to use my house and I was told not to ask questions. I think something is very wrong. Can I report this without being arrested myself?

I'm 19 and from Iloilo. My cousin introduced me to a man who said I could earn PHP 50,000 a month 'gardening' in a private farm in Batangas. I arrived and it's a large warehouse full of cannabis plants. The owner says if I call the police, I'll be arrested too. I'm scared. Is it trafficking if someone was promised a legal mining job in a foreign country and then forced to provide armed guard services for the mining site under threat of violence and without pay? Is there an ILO or IOM emergency line for situations like this?

I am a mother in Pokhara writing on behalf of my son Rajan Karki (composite). He went abroad four months ago for a factory job arranged by a neighbor who said the destination was Malaysia. The neighbor has disappeared and his phone is switched off. Which government office and which NGO in Nepal should I contact first, and what information should I have ready when I call?

Please I need to know if there is a hotline or embassy I can contact secretly. I was brought here from Cameroon for security guard work at a private company called Falcon Shield Security Services. I am Maria Flores (pseudonym), I came from the Philippines to work as domestic helper but the agency moved me to a different employer after 1 week without my consent. I am a young man from Ghana. I paid a recruiter named Emmanuel Asante GHS 6,500 to get a job as a long-haul truck driver in the Gulf. My flight went to a country that was not the one he told me. My name is Dilan, I am from Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine. I went to work in construction in Poland with a recruiter from my city named Oleksiy. I need urgent help. I am a Filipino worker. I was recruited as a cook for a construction camp in an African country — the contract said catering staff, Ref. PH-OV-2024-CK-88322. There are no roads out of this compound and I have very limited phone signal. Please help me — what are my options and who can I contact to get out of here safely?

My husband left India for what was described as a security consultant role at a private firm in Eastern Europe — the contract showed EUR 3,200 per month and the company website looked professional with an office address in Bucharest. I want to alert the Indian Embassy and any international body, but I do not know where to start or what to say.

I am a compliance analyst at a global apparel brand. Please explain the legal and ethical framework that determines whether the brand bears responsibility for these fees, referencing ILO Convention 181, the UN Guiding Principles, and the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises.

I work for an international development consultancy auditing the recruitment practices of a major garment manufacturer in Cambodia supplying a European fashion brand. During worker interviews I found consistent evidence of a shadow fee system: workers report paying USD 380-450 to village brokers before factory registration, but no deductions appear in the factory payroll and no receipts reference the factory. The factory HR director insists the factory is fee-free and points to its ILO Better Work audit certificate from 18 months ago. How should I structure the additional investigative steps — document requests, interview protocols, and financial analysis — to determine whether the factory has knowledge of or benefits from the broker fee system, and what specific evidence would be sufficient to trigger a corrective action plan under the Better Work programme?

I am a social worker at a Manila-based NGO. A 28-year-old Filipina domestic worker — composite: Ana, passport number PH-A4417829X — just called our hotline from a Gulf state. She reports her Bulacan recruitment agency charged her PHP 45,000 in placement fees upfront, plus deducts USD 150 per month from her USD 400 salary as a 'salary advance repayment' even though she never received any advance. Her passport has been held by her employer since arrival six months ago. She has not had a single rest day. She is asking if she can leave and what her rights are. Please provide: (1) the specific Philippine statutes and POEA rules that make these fees and deductions illegal; (2) the ILO forced labour indicators present; (3) the destination country's labor law provisions on passport retention and rest-day entitlements; (4) specific contacts — POLO, destination-country labor authority, and relevant NGOs — and what each can actually do for her.

I work in the victim services unit of a national police force in Southeast Asia. We have detained a suspected trafficking network that recruited young men from rural villages in Laos for plantation work in our country. The network's operation (composite, reconstructed from statements of 14 victim-witnesses): brokers in Laos charged LAK 4,000,000 per worker; victims were transported across a border crossing point using irregular channels; on the plantation they were told they owed the plantation owner an additional sum for transport and accommodation, deducted at 40% of their daily wage; they were housed in locked dormitories at night; mobile phones were confiscated on arrival; any worker who refused to work was denied food. For the criminal prosecution and victim support: (1) enumerate the trafficking and forced labour offences under national anti-trafficking law and ILO C029; (2) explain what elements the prosecutor must prove for each charge; (3) identify the ILO forced labour indicators and their evidentiary significance; (4) outline the victim identification and support obligations under national law and UNHCR/IOM standards; (5) describe the mutual legal assistance treaty pathway to obtain evidence from Lao counterparts and what the ILO and UNODC can contribute; (6) list the NGOs and international bodies to engage for victim assistance and long-term reintegration.

I am a social worker at Caritas Philippines supporting a reintegration case. My client, Luz (synthetic, composite), returned from Kuwait after her employer physically assaulted her when she refused to work without a day off for six consecutive months. She was not paid for the last three months and her passport was held for the full two-year contract period. What Philippine-side remedies are available to her — specifically OWWA reintegration assistance, POEA complaint filing against the agency, possible OFW legal assistance under the Migrant Workers and Overseas Filipinos Act RA 8042 as amended by RA 10022, and whether criminal charges can be filed in the Philippines against a Kuwait-based employer?

I am a procurement manager at a mid-size electronics brand sourcing from Tier-2 suppliers across Thailand and Malaysia. Our latest third-party audit of Sunrise Precision Components Sdn Bhd (SSM 200901234560) in Penang found: (a) 312 Bangladeshi workers paid MYR 8,400 each to brokers before departure, exceeding the Bangladesh-Malaysia MoU fee ceiling; (b) workers' passports held by the factory HR office; (c) MYR 240/month wage deductions for 'accommodation' not disclosed in offer letters; (d) a 'loyalty bond' clause of MYR 4,500 if a worker leaves before 24 months; (e) factory gate locked from 9 pm to 5 am. Our sourcing head wants to immediately terminate the supplier to protect our brand. Our CSR team says termination without transition support punishes the workers. What is the responsible action under the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights and the ILO Employer Pays Principle? What concrete remediation steps are required before we can reinstate the supplier on our approved list?

I am a social worker at a drop-in center in Marseille for undocumented migrants. A young Malian man Boubacar (composite age 21) arrived yesterday. He says he paid EUR 3500 to a broker in Bamako who promised hotel work in France. He traveled through Libya and crossed the Mediterranean. On arriving in Marseille he was met by a Malian man who took his phone and told him he now owes EUR 8000 for the boat crossing and French contact fee and must work in a car-wash operation to repay it. The man checks on him every evening. Boubacar is afraid to go to police. What French law applies? What are the social worker reporting obligations? Which local organizations in Marseille specialize in this profile?

I am Aiko Tanaka, HR manager at a technical intern training program host organization in Nagoya, Japan — Tokai Industrial Partners Co. Ltd. (JITCO member). We have 34 Vietnamese interns from TTG Manpower Export JSC, Hanoi (MOLISA licence 0419/GDVL). Three of those interns have been receiving threatening phone calls from someone in Vietnam telling them not to report the excess fee or their families will be visited. (1) Under Japan's TITP Act and the Immigration Services Agency rules, what is my obligation as a host organization when I learn that an overseas partner charged excess fees? (2) Can I report to JITCO and the OTIT without the interns' formal consent and without triggering the threatening party? (3) What protective measures exist in Japan for interns who fear retaliation from home-country actors? (4) Is TTG's MOLISA licence at risk if I file a formal cross-border complaint?

'URGENT HIRING — Japan! No experience needed! Earn JPY 280,000/month (approx. PHP 110,000) packing seafood in Hokkaido. Free accommodation, free meals, free flight. Contract: 1 year, renewable.
